title: The Startup Decision
description: Navigate the high-stakes journey of building a startup from a raw idea to product launch. Every decision shapes your runway, your team, and your shot at success.
theme: Building a startup from idea to launch
learning_objectives: Understand how strategic planning affects startup survival
Practice making calculated risk decisions under resource constraints
Develop resilience when pivoting under pressure
Build awareness of the trade-offs between speed and thoroughness
Recognise when to trust instincts vs. seek external validation
learning_concept: Every startup decision is a bet — the best founders learn to make informed bets quickly, adapt without panic, and protect their runway while chasing their vision.
psychological_framework: Effectuation Theory (Sarasvathy) — means-based thinking, affordable loss, and co-creation under uncertainty

chapters.title: The Idea
chapters.teaser: You have an idea that could change everything — but do you have what it takes to pursue it?

chapters.title: The Build
chapters.teaser: The product is taking shape but the runway is shrinking fast...

chapters.title: The Launch
chapters.teaser: Launch day is here — will the world embrace what you've built?

chapters.title: The Scale
chapters.teaser: The product works. But scaling it might break everything that made it work.

chapters.title: The Founder's Choice
chapters.teaser: The startup is real. The question now is: what kind of company — and founder — do you want to be?

glossary_terms.definition: The amount of time a startup can operate before running out of money, based on current spending.
The simplest version of a product that allows you to collect validated learning about customers with minimal effort.
A structured course correction to test a new fundamental hypothesis about the product, strategy, or business model.
Evidence that a startup's product is gaining customers and growing, often measured by sign-ups, revenue, or active users.
The speed at which a company spends its available capital before generating positive cash flow.
The degree to which a product satisfies a strong market demand — the moment customers love what you built.
The tendency for a product to accumulate more and more features over time, often losing focus on its core value proposition.
Financial technology — companies that use digital tools to improve or automate financial services like payments, lending, and credit.
A small neighbourhood retail shop in India, typically family-owned, serving as the backbone of Indian retail with over 12 million stores nationwide.
A concise declaration of a company's purpose, values, and the change it seeks to create in the world.
A formal gathering of a company's board of directors to discuss strategy, governance, and major decisions.

scenes.title: The Spark
scenes.narrative: It's 2 AM in your Bengaluru apartment, and you've just built a rough prototype of an app that helps kirana store owners manage inventory using WhatsApp. Your friend Priya, who co-founded a failed SaaS company last year, sits across from you. 'You need to quit your job and do this full-time,' she says. 'Or someone else will.' Your stable ₹18 LPA job at an MNC stares back at you from your laptop screen. The prototype is rough, but the idea feels like lightning.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian entrepreneur at a laptop in a cluttered Bengaluru apartment at night, a rough app prototype on screen, a friend leaning over looking excited, city lights through the window, warm dramatic lighting, photorealistic digital art
scenes.coaching_moment: The decision to go all-in on an idea is one of the highest-stakes bets an entrepreneur makes. Clarity about your 'why' matters more than certainty about your 'how'.
scenes.reflection_prompt: What would it take for you to leave a stable career to pursue an uncertain idea?

choices.label: Quit and go all-in — the idea is too good to build on weekends
choices.description: Maximum commitment. Maximum risk.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for risk tolerance, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Maximum commitment. Maximum risk.

choices.label: Keep the job but give yourself 90 days to validate with 10 real users
choices.description: Disciplined approach — test before you leap.

choices.label: Talk to 20 kirana owners this weekend before deciding anything
choices.description: Customer discovery first. Excitement can wait.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You leaned into playing the long game — but this moment rewards reading the room first — strategy without people is just a spreadsheet. Customer discovery first. Excitement can wait.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Co-Founder Question
scenes.narrative: Word spreads fast. Rohan, your IIT batchmate and a brilliant full-stack developer, reaches out. 'I want in,' he says over coffee in Koramangala. 'I'll take 40% equity.' You like Rohan — he's technically outstanding. But 40% feels steep for someone joining after you've already built the prototype, and you've heard he can be controlling under pressure. Another option: hire a contract developer at ₹2 lakh/month, burning runway but keeping full control.
scenes.image_prompt: Two young Indian founders shaking hands over coffee in a Bengaluru cafe, startup whiteboards and laptops visible, warm afternoon light, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Co-founder relationships are like marriages — getting the equity split, trust, and working style right early prevents catastrophic breakdowns later.

choices.label: Accept Rohan's offer — great tech co-founders are rare
choices.description: Speed of build matters. Share the pie.

choices.label: Counter-offer 20% with a 1-year vesting cliff
choices.description: Protect your cap table while keeping Rohan interested.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for delayed gratification, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Protect your cap table while keeping Rohan interested.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Angel Offer
scenes.narrative: A well-known angel investor, Meera Kapoor, DMs you on LinkedIn after seeing your product demo at a startup event. She's offering ₹50 lakh for 15% equity — standard early-stage terms. But there's a catch: she wants a decision by Friday and expects weekly updates and board observer rights. Your gut says the money would be transformative, but the timeline pressure and ongoing oversight make you uneasy.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian entrepreneur reading an investment offer on a phone in a busy Mumbai co-working space, looking thoughtful and slightly stressed, modern office setting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Early funding accelerates your path but also changes the nature of your startup. Know what you are trading when you take outside capital.
scenes.reflection_prompt: Is urgency a manipulation tactic or a genuine test of your conviction?

choices.label: Accept the offer — ₹50 lakh solves your immediate runway problem
choices.description: Security and speed. The oversight is manageable.

choices.label: Ask for two more weeks to do due diligence on Meera
choices.description: Investors should be evaluated too — this is a long-term relationship.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for delayed gratification, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Investors should be evaluated too — this is a long-term relationship.

choices.label: Politely decline — you want to grow on revenue before taking equity dilution
choices.description: Bootstrapper mindset. Risky but fully on your terms.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Bootstrapper mindset. Risky but fully on your terms.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: Build vs. Buy
scenes.narrative: Three months in. The product is 60% built but your burn rate is climbing. Rohan suggests integrating a third-party inventory API — it will save six weeks of development time but costs ₹80,000/month in licensing fees and creates a technical dependency you can't control. Alternatively, you build it from scratch: slower, harder, but you own it entirely. The first paying pilot, a group of 5 kirana stores in Indiranagar, is watching your progress.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian developer reviewing code on dual monitors in a startup office, whiteboard with architecture diagrams behind, team members in discussion, warm focused lighting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Build vs. buy decisions reveal your long-term strategy. Short-term speed often trades off against long-term control and cost.

choices.label: Use the third-party API to ship faster and impress the pilot users
choices.description: Time-to-market is everything right now.

choices.label: Build in-house even if the pilot waits an extra month
choices.description: Own the architecture. Own the future.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for delayed gratification, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Own the architecture. Own the future.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Hiring Pressure
scenes.narrative: Your pilot users love the product — but they're asking for features faster than you and Rohan can build. You have two options: hire two junior developers at ₹6 lakh each to speed up delivery, or say no to some features and focus ruthlessly on the core use case. Priya calls to warn you: 'I hired too fast — it killed us. Culture broke down in six months.' But your pilot users are getting impatient.
scenes.image_prompt: Startup team in an intense brainstorming session, sticky notes on walls, laptops everywhere, one leader at the whiteboard, Indian urban setting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Premature scaling is one of the top reasons startups fail. Saying no to good ideas to protect your core is a leadership skill, not a weakness.
scenes.reflection_prompt: How do you decide when to grow a team versus staying lean?

choices.label: Hire two junior devs — growth requires investment in people
choices.description: Scale up now while momentum is high.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for risk tolerance, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Scale up now while momentum is high.

choices.label: Decline new feature requests and double down on the core product
choices.description: Depth before breadth. Earn trust through excellence.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for delayed gratification, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Depth before breadth. Earn trust through excellence.

choices.label: Bring in one experienced senior developer on contract
choices.description: The middle path — quality without overcommitting.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Competitor Appears
scenes.narrative: A well-funded startup from Delhi — backed by a Tier-1 VC — launches a similar product with a splashy press release and a free 6-month trial. Your pilot users start WhatsApp-ing you nervously. Rohan wants to slash your pricing to compete. You know that racing to the bottom on pricing could permanently damage your brand positioning and unit economics. This is the moment that separates founders from dreamers.
scenes.image_prompt: Startup founder staring at a competitor's press release on a laptop, team gathered around with worried faces, whiteboard with strategy options, tension visible, Indian co-working space, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: The best response to competition is not to react — it is to out-execute on the dimensions your competitor cannot easily copy.

choices.label: Match their pricing — you can't afford to lose pilot users
choices.description: Protect market share now, fix economics later.

choices.label: Differentiate on service — offer white-glove onboarding your competitor can't
choices.description: Win on experience, not on price.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You leaned into playing the long game — but this moment rewards reading the room first — strategy without people is just a spreadsheet. Win on experience, not on price.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: Launch Day Chaos
scenes.narrative: Launch day arrives. You've sent press releases, lined up a launch on Product Hunt, and your 5 pilot stores have agreed to give testimonials. At 9 AM your servers buckle under unexpected traffic — 400 concurrent users when you designed for 100. Rohan is furiously patching. An influential tech journalist tweets that your app is 'down on launch day' — and the tweet is getting traction. Your phone won't stop buzzing.
scenes.image_prompt: Frantic startup team hunched over laptops with server error screens, phones buzzing, one founder on a call, tension and excitement mixed, modern Indian tech office, dramatic lighting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: How a founder responds to a public crisis defines their reputation more than the crisis itself. Transparency builds trust; silence destroys it.

choices.label: Post a transparent update publicly — 'We're experiencing high demand, working on a fix'
choices.description: Own the moment. Turn a failure into a story of growth.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Own the moment. Turn a failure into a story of growth.

choices.label: Go silent and fix it first — don't amplify the problem
choices.description: Fix, then communicate. Accuracy over speed.

choices.label: Personally call every pilot user and promise them priority access once stable
choices.description: High-touch relationship management in a crisis.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for empathy, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. High-touch relationship management in a crisis.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Acquisition Offer
scenes.narrative: Two weeks post-launch, you have 80 paying stores and ₹3.2 lakh in MRR. Then an email arrives from a large retail-tech company: they want to acquire your startup for ₹4 crore. For you personally that's life-changing money. But Rohan thinks you should turn it down — he believes you can reach ₹50 crore valuation in 18 months if you raise a Series A. Meera Kapoor, your angel investor, would receive a 3x return and is silently supportive of either path.
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian founder sitting alone in a quiet office after everyone has left, acquisition offer letter on the table, looking at city lights through a window, contemplative mood, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: There is no objectively right answer between a certain outcome and an uncertain but larger one. The right choice depends on your personal risk tolerance and life goals.
scenes.reflection_prompt: What would you weigh more — financial security today or the chance to build something much larger?

choices.label: Accept the acquisition — ₹4 crore is a real outcome for a 6-month-old startup
choices.description: A good exit beats a great ambition that never materialises.

choices.label: Decline and raise a Series A — you're just getting started
choices.description: Bet on yourself and the bigger vision.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for risk tolerance, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Bet on yourself and the bigger vision.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Reflection
scenes.narrative: Months later, you sit in your Bengaluru apartment — the same one where this all started at 2 AM. Whether you sold or kept building, the journey has fundamentally changed you. You understand now that startups are not about the outcome — they are about who you become in the process. The kirana stores you helped are thriving. You have a list of everything you would do differently. And a new idea is already forming in the back of your mind.
scenes.image_prompt: A reflective Indian entrepreneur sitting by a window at dusk, city lights below, journal open, calm and purposeful expression, warm contemplative lighting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Every startup journey, regardless of outcome, is a masterclass in decision-making under uncertainty. The real product you built was yourself.
scenes.reflection_prompt: What is one belief about success that this journey has changed for you?

choices.label: 'I learned that resilience means adapting, not just enduring'
choices.description: A hard-won understanding of what persistence really means.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. A hard-won understanding of what persistence really means.

choices.label: 'I should have listened to customers more and my assumptions less'
choices.description: Honest self-assessment is the foundation of the next attempt.

choices.label: 'I took on too much risk too fast — I need a more systematic approach'
choices.description: A learning path that leads to a more structured next venture.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for delayed gratification, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. A learning path that leads to a more structured next venture.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The 100th Store
scenes.narrative: Three months post-launch. You have 100 kirana stores on the platform, generating ₹5 lakh MRR. The WhatsApp support group for your store owners is exploding with feature requests. Rohan wants to build a full inventory management suite. Priya warns: 'Feature creep killed my last startup. Stay focused.' Meanwhile, a major FMCG brand has reached out — they want to use your data to understand kirana buying patterns. It could be a massive new revenue stream but would mean selling your store owners' data.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian startup founders celebrating 100 customers while simultaneously facing strategic decisions on a whiteboard, growth charts and feature requests visible, modern office, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: At the inflection point between product-market fit and scale, the decisions you make about what you will NOT do matter as much as the decisions about what you will.

choices.label: Reject the data deal — your store owners' trust is not for sale, no matter the revenue
choices.description: Ethical floor. Protect the relationship that is your moat.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for ethical reasoning, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Ethical floor. Protect the relationship that is your moat.

choices.label: Explore the FMCG partnership with full transparency to store owners — let them opt in
choices.description: Ethical data use with consent. Revenue and trust together.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Team Breaking Point
scenes.narrative: Your three-person engineering team is burning out. Rohan has not taken a day off in 47 days. The two junior developers are making mistakes from exhaustion. Customer support tickets are piling up. You need to either hire aggressively — spending precious runway — or slow growth to match your team's capacity. A mentor tells you: 'The graveyard of startups is full of companies that grew faster than their teams could sustain.'
scenes.image_prompt: Exhausted small startup team late at night, energy drinks and code on screens, one person with head down, founder looking worried, Indian co-working space, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: A founder who burns out their team in pursuit of growth metrics is borrowing from the future at an interest rate they cannot afford.
scenes.reflection_prompt: What is the true cost of pushing a team past their breaking point?

choices.label: Mandate a one-week team break and cap working hours at 50/week going forward
choices.description: Protect the people. Sustainable pace wins the marathon.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for empathy, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Protect the people. Sustainable pace wins the marathon.

choices.label: Hire three new team members immediately — the growth justifies the investment in people
choices.description: Scale the team to match the demand. Invest in capacity.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Pivot Within the Pivot
scenes.narrative: User data reveals something surprising: 60% of your most active kirana stores are using the app primarily for credit management — tracking which customers owe them money — not inventory. The feature you built as an afterthought has become the killer use case. Rohan is excited: 'We might actually be a fintech company, not a SaaS company.' The implications are enormous — different investors, different regulations, different competition. Priya asks the critical question: 'Do we follow the data, or do we stick with the vision we raised money on?'
scenes.image_prompt: Startup founders staring at unexpected user data on a dashboard showing credit management as the top feature, surprised and excited expressions, data visualizations, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: The best founders hold their vision loosely enough to let the market teach them what they are actually building.

choices.label: Follow the data — pivot the positioning to kirana credit management and explore fintech partnerships
choices.description: The market is telling you who you are. Listen.

choices.label: Keep the original vision but enhance the credit feature as a retention tool within the inventory platform
choices.description: Integrate, do not pivot. Add the popular feature without losing identity.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You leaned into playing the long game — but this moment rewards reading the room first — strategy without people is just a spreadsheet. Integrate, do not pivot. Add the popular feature without losing identity.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Mission Statement
scenes.narrative: Meera Kapoor calls a board meeting and asks the question every growing startup must eventually answer: 'What is your mission? Not your product, not your metrics — your mission. What change are you trying to create in the world?' You and Rohan look at each other. You have been so busy building and surviving that you never formally articulated why. But the answer matters — it will guide every hiring decision, partnership, and product choice from here forward.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian startup founders in a board meeting being asked a fundamental question about mission, thoughtful expressions, whiteboard with company values being drafted, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: A company without a clear mission eventually optimises for the wrong thing. The mission does not need to be grandiose — it needs to be true.

choices.label: 'We exist to give India's 12 million kirana stores the same digital tools that large retailers have — levelling the playing field'
choices.description: Democratisation. Technology as equaliser. A mission worth fighting for.

choices.label: 'We exist to build the most trusted technology relationship in Indian retail — where the store owner comes first, always'
choices.description: Trust-first. A values-driven mission that shapes culture.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for empathy, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Trust-first. A values-driven mission that shapes culture.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Personal Cost
scenes.narrative: Your mother calls on a Sunday evening. 'Beta, we have not seen you in four months. Your father asks about you every day.' You realise with a jolt that you have been so consumed by the startup that you have neglected the people who matter most. Rohan mentions that his relationship ended last month — he did not even have time to process it. The startup is growing, but the founders are shrinking. Priya was right: 'Build a company that does not require you to destroy yourself to run it.'
scenes.image_prompt: Indian startup founder on a phone call with worried parents, looking at family photos, realising the personal cost of entrepreneurship, quiet evening, emotional moment, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: A startup that requires you to sacrifice every relationship and every moment of rest to survive is not a sustainable business — it is an addiction with a business plan.

choices.label: Block one weekend per month as a non-negotiable family and personal time — protect it like a board meeting
choices.description: Boundaries are not weakness. They are infrastructure for long-term performance.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. Boundaries are not weakness. They are infrastructure for long-term performance.

choices.label: Visit your parents this weekend and have an honest conversation about what you are building and why
choices.description: Reconnect. Let the people who love you understand your world.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

scenes.title: The Anniversary
scenes.narrative: One year since the 2 AM prototype. You are no longer a person with an idea — you are a founder with a company, a team, a product used by real businesses, and a set of scars that no MBA programme could have given you. You sit in your Bengaluru apartment — the same one — and look at the first sketch of the app on a Post-it note still stuck to the wall. The sketch looks nothing like what the product became. Neither do you. Rohan texts: 'Same bat-time, same bat-channel? We have a long road ahead.' You smile. For the first time, the road ahead does not feel like a threat. It feels like a promise.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian entrepreneur in the same apartment where it all started, looking at an old Post-it sketch of the original app, the actual app on a laptop showing real users, one year of growth visible in small details, warm nostalgic light, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Every founder starts with an idea. The ones who endure start with an idea and end up with character. The company is the vehicle — your growth as a human being is the destination.

choices.label: 'The startup did not make me a better entrepreneur. It made me a better person. And that is why it will survive'
choices.description: The deepest lesson: personal growth and business growth are the same thing.
choices.ending_message: From a 2 AM prototype to 100+ kirana stores, from a stable job to a founder's scars, from uncertainty to purpose — you built something real. Not just a product, but a set of values, a team that trusts you, and a version of yourself that can handle whatever comes next. The road is long. You are ready for it.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with strategic thinking. The deepest lesson: personal growth and business growth are the same thing.

choices.label: 'I would make half the same decisions and half completely different ones — and that is exactly the right ratio'
choices.description: Honest self-assessment: the mark of a founder who will keep getting better.
choices.ending_message: Fifty-fifty is the honest founder's scorecard. Half right, half wrong, all learned. The willingness to hold that complexity — to celebrate the wins without hiding from the mistakes — is what separates founders who build one company from founders who build careers. The next chapter starts now.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: strategic thinking.

coaching_moment: Every startup decision is a bet — the best founders learn to make informed bets quickly, adapt without panic, and protect their runway while chasing their vision.
cultural_context: India produces over 100,000 new startups annually, but most face difficult early-stage decisions about product direction, team composition, and funding. This game develops the strategic decision-making that separates founders who succeed from those who fail at the first obstacle.

hallmarks: Validates demand with real customers before quitting a paying job
Says no to the first cheque if the terms are wrong — keeps optionality
Treats co-founder dynamics as the #1 risk to manage, ahead of product or market
Makes the smallest reversible bet that produces the biggest information gain
Falls for the romance of the leap before validating that anyone wants the thing
Takes whatever capital is offered when 'no' would have been the right answer
Lets the co-founder relationship drift instead of having the hard conversation early
Burns runway on the wrong things — usually growth before product-market fit

challenge_persona_ladder: a founder-friend who has been through it twice, asking the questions you don't want to answer
an early-stage investor at a Series Seed pitch, pushing on numbers, comparing you to better-prepared rivals
your most skeptical co-founder candidate doing a final reference check on whether to risk their career on you

reflection_prompt: Looking back at the choices you made, which one felt hardest and why? What would you do differently if you replayed?
